 By City News Service | news@socalnews.com and Ryanne Mena | rmena@scng.com PUBLISHED: October 19, 2026 at 3:24 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 20, 2026 at 2:55 PM PDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... A strong October storm was moving toward Southern California Tuesday, Oct. 20, with forecasters warning of widespread rain, possible thunderstorms and an increasing risk of localized flooding.
 “The system is starting to turn the corner and head east and seems to be on track for a relatively on time arrival … by afternoon in LA County,” according to the National Weather Service.
 Forecasters said rainfall totals across much of Los Angeles County are expected to average about 1.5 inches, with 2 to 3 inches possible in areas where terrain enhances rainfall and in locations hit by thunderstorms.
 The NWS issued a flood watch Tuesday for the Malibu coast and eastern and western Santa Monica Mountains, effective Wednesday afternoon through Thursday afternoon. The watch includes Malibu, Malibu Bowl, Pacific Palisades and Topanga.
 “A targeted Flood Watch has been issued for … the Santa Monica Mountains and adjacent coastline as models have been indicating the highest rain rates in those areas, around .75″ per hour,” according to the NWS.
 Since an excessive amount of rain isn’t expected to hit Malibu’s burn scars, city officials aren’t worried “but we are prepared,” said the city’s spokesperson, Matt Meyerhoff.
 The city will be putting out emergency alerts to local residents through social media and their website to warm people about incoming stormy conditions, he added.
 “I think it’s fairly safe to say that we could expect at least some minor debris flow in the area,” said Bryan Lewis, a meteorologist with the NWS.
 Debris flows are also a potential event meteorologists are looking out for near other burn scars left by the Palisades and Eaton fires, but because they’re not considered fresh burn scars, it would take more rain to cause debris flows.
 Flooding could occur in urban and poor-drainage areas, with extensive street flooding and flooding of creeks and rivers possible.
 Forecasters said “there is a small (5% or less) chance of a weak tornado as the upper low moves inland late Wednesday night into Thursday morning.”
 The storm is expected to bring a significant drop in temperatures following several days of unusually hot weather and powerful Santa Ana winds. Wednesday and Thursday are expected to be cloudy and cool, with daytime highs generally in the mid-60s to lower 70s across much of Los Angeles County.
 Orange County is also expected to experience cooler temperatures and periods of rain, with thunderstorms possible as the storm moves through Southern California.
 Forecasters said snow is unlikely below 8,000 feet.
 Marine conditions could also deteriorate Wednesday and Thursday, with thunderstorms and isolated waterspouts possible in coastal waters. The NWS warned that thunderstorms over the ocean could produce lightning, gusty and erratic winds, small hail and choppy seas.
 A beach hazards statement remains in effect through late Thursday night for portions of the Los Angeles County coastline, according to the weather service. Elevated surf and dangerous rip currents are expected, with minor beach erosion and tidal overflow possible in low-lying areas.
 Dry weather is expected to return Friday, followed by another round of offshore Santa Ana winds over the weekend. The NWS said the upcoming Santa Ana event would be weaker than last week’s, with wind gusts of 30 to 50 mph possible, strongest in the mountains.
 Temperatures are expected to rebound into the upper 70s and 80s across most coastal and valley areas over the weekend, forecasters said.
 Graphic courtesy of the National Weather Service 
 Over in the Inland Empire, temperatures on Wednesday are expected to be in the high 70s, with a cooler Thursday of highs in the 60s, said Kyle Wheeler, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. Temperatures will begin to gradually increase on Friday with a high of 73, sunny skies and a high of 78 on Saturday, and a high of 80 degrees on Sunday, said Paul Steward, a lead meteorologist with the NWS.
 San Bernardino and Riverside county residents can expect to see half an inch to up inch of rain over the next couple of days.
 There’s a 15-20% chance for thunderstorms Wednesday night. If that does develop, residents can expect to see heavy rain and winds with gusts of 40-60 mph.
 Meteorologists are keeping an eye on burn scars left by the Bridge and Line fires from 2024, though they’re not expecting enough rain to create debris flows.
